passages.t: Arise, shine: the nations come to the light
passages.happening:
‘Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD rises upon you’ (verse 1). Darkness covers the earth and thick darkness the peoples, but the LORD will rise on Zion (verse 2). ‘Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn’ (verse 3).

Zion is to lift her eyes and look. Her sons come from far away, and her daughters are carried on the arm (verse 4). She will be radiant, her heart will swell with joy, because the riches of the sea and the wealth of the nations will come to her (verse 5).

‘Caravans of camels will cover your land’ (verse 6), from Midian, Ephah and Sheba, ‘bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD’ (verse 6). The flocks of Kedar and the rams of Nebaioth will be offered on God's altar (verse 7). Who are these that fly like clouds, like doves to their shelters (verse 8)? The ships of Tarshish lead the way, bringing Zion's children home with silver and gold, to the honor of the LORD (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 59 ended with the Redeemer coming to Zion. Chapter 60 describes his arrival as a sunrise. It is the first of three chapters, 60 to 62, that form the bright center of the last part of Isaiah.

For those who came back after 539 BC, Jerusalem was a humble place. The rebuilt temple, finished about 516 or 515 BC, was plainer than Solomon's, and older people wept when they saw its foundation. The walls lay in ruins until Nehemiah rebuilt them around 445 BC. Judah was a small Persian province. Against that background, a chapter promising that nations would bring their wealth to Jerusalem would have sounded almost too much, and that is part of its force.

The peoples named are real. Midian and Ephah were desert tribes descended from Abraham through Keturah. Sheba, in southern Arabia, was famous for gold, spices and incense, and its queen once came to Solomon. Kedar and Nebaioth were Arab tribes descended from Ishmael. Tarshish was a distant port reached by large ships, often placed in the far west of the Mediterranean, though its location is debated. Frankincense, a fragrant resin from southern Arabia, was burned in temple worship.
passages.later: Isaiah had seen it from the start: ‘many peoples will come and say’ that they will go up to the mountain of the LORD (Isaiah 2:3). Sheba's queen once came to Solomon ‘with camels bearing spices, gold in great abundance, and precious stones’ (1 Kings 10:2).
passages.asks: Zion is told to shine because light has come to her, not because she made it. Ask what it would mean for you to rise and shine with a light you did not produce. And ask who is still in thick darkness around you.

passages.t: Gates always open, and oppressors bowing
passages.happening:
‘Foreigners will rebuild your walls, and their kings will serve you’ (verse 10). God struck Zion in anger, ‘yet in favor I will show you mercy’ (verse 10). ‘Your gates will always stand open; they will never be shut, day or night’ (verse 11), so that the wealth of the nations may come in.

The nation or kingdom that will not serve her will perish (verse 12). The glory of Lebanon, its cypress and elm and boxwood, will come to adorn God's sanctuary (verse 13). The sons of her oppressors will come and bow down to her and call her ‘the City of the LORD, Zion of the Holy One of Israel’ (verse 14).

She was forsaken and despised, with no one passing through, but God will make her ‘an everlasting pride, a joy from age to age’ (verse 15). She will drink the milk of nations and know that the LORD is her Savior and her Redeemer (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
In a world of warfare, a city's gates were shut at night and in danger. Gates open day and night meant complete safety and constant welcome.

Timber from Lebanon, cedar and cypress, was the prized building material for palaces and temples. Solomon brought it in for the first temple. Here the goods of the world flow toward God's house, not toward an emperor's capital.

Nations bowing at someone's feet was the standard picture of submission to a conqueror. Verse 14 reverses Jerusalem's humiliation by those who had crushed her.

The poem speaks to Zion as a woman throughout. Forsaken and despised, she becomes a joy from age to age.
passages.later: Revelation takes up verse 11 for the new Jerusalem: ‘Its gates will never be shut at the end of the day, because there will be no night there’ (Revelation 21:25). ‘And into the city will be brought the glory and honor of the nations’ (Revelation 21:26).
passages.hard:
Is this chapter promising that one people will rule over the others?

Some verses, read alone, sound like a reversal of empire: nations serve Zion, kings bow, and the nation that will not serve will perish (verse 12). Readers respond differently. Some Jewish and Christian interpreters read the chapter as a promise of Israel's literal restoration and preeminence in the age to come. Many others note that its center is not Zion's power but God's glory. The nations come to the light of the LORD, bring gifts for his house and proclaim his praises (verse 6), and the result is peace and righteousness, not violence (verses 17 and 18). On this reading, bowing is the ancient way of acknowledging the true king, and those who come are worshipers, not slaves. The chapter belongs with 2:2-4 and 56:6-7, where the nations join Israel in worship.

What the chapter plainly rejects is a world where Zion is forsaken and violence rules. It gives no warrant to any people or nation today to claim power over others in God's name.
passages.asks: Zion's gates stand open day and night. Ask whether your home, your church or your heart keeps its gates open or shut. And ask what it means to you that God's answer to a despised city is joy from age to age.

passages.happening:
‘Instead of bronze I will bring you gold; I will bring silver in place of iron’ (verse 17). ‘I will appoint peace as your governor and righteousness as your ruler’ (verse 17). ‘No longer will violence be heard in your land, nor ruin or destruction within your borders’ (verse 18). ‘But you will name your walls Salvation and your gates Praise’ (verse 18).

The sun will no longer be her light by day, nor the moon by night, ‘for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your splendor’ (verse 19). Her sun will not set, ‘and the days of your sorrow will cease’ (verse 20).

All her people will be righteous and possess the land forever. ‘They are the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, so that I may be glorified’ (verse 21). ‘The least of you will become a thousand, and the smallest a mighty nation’ (verse 22). ‘I am the LORD; in its time I will accomplish it quickly’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is framed by light. It opens with light rising on Zion and closes with the LORD himself as her light, replacing sun and moon.

Verses 17 and 18 are a list of exchanges, each old thing replaced by something better: bronze with gold, iron with silver, violence with peace. Peace becomes the governor, and righteousness the ruler.

Naming walls and gates followed the old custom of giving city gates names, as Jerusalem's gates had in Nehemiah's day. Here the names are Salvation and Praise.

Glory, kavod, comes from a word for heavy. God's glory is the weight and splendor of his presence, which filled the tabernacle and Solomon's temple, and which Ezekiel had seen leave the temple before the exile. Now it rises on Zion like the sun.
passages.later: Revelation says of the new Jerusalem, ‘the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, because the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp’ (Revelation 21:23). Ezekiel had watched the glory leave the temple (Ezekiel 10).
passages.asks: God promises that the days of sorrow will cease. Ask what sorrow you most long to see end, and whether you can hope for it in God's time. And ask what it would look like for peace to govern your home.
